TRANSCRIPT OF PROCEEDINGS
THE HON CATHERINE HOLMES AC SC, Commissioner
THE ROYAL COMMISSION INTO THE ROBODEBT SCHEME
WEDNESDAY, 7 DECEMBER 2022 AT 10.02 AM (AEST)
DAY 15
MR JUSTIN GREGGERY KC, Senior Counsel Assisting
MS SALWA MARSH, Counsel Assisting
MS DOMINIQUE HOGAN-DORAN SC, for the Commonwealth
MR TRENT GLOVER, for the Commonwealth

COMMISSIONER: Shall we get the appearances for the day, Mr Greggery?
MR GREGGERY: Yes. If it pleases the Commission, I appear with Ms Marsh today.
COMMISSIONER: Thank you.
MS HOGAN-DORAN: May it please the Commission, I appear with Mr Glover today.
COMMISSIONER: Thank you. Yes, Mr Greggery.
MR GREGGERY: Yes. Ms Campbell has returned to resume her evidence. But before I start
with her, can I update the Commission on a procedural matter.
COMMISSIONER: Yes.
MR GREGGERY: Last night there was correspondence between the Solicitors Assisting the
Commission and the Solicitors Assisting the Commonwealth in respect of the Ombudsman.
The update is that the Ombudsman's Office is prepared to voluntarily assist the Commission
and provide documents to Ms Louise Macleod, who was involved in early 2017, and it is
anticipated that Ms Macleod is willing to give a Statement and assist the Commission in
Hearing Block 3.
COMMISSIONER: Thank you.
MR GREGGERY: Ms Campbell, I think, remains under her former -
COMMISSIONER: Yes. You understand that, Ms Campbell. Thank you.
MR GREGGERY: Thank you. Yes.
<KATHRYN CAMPBELL, ON FORMER OATH
<EXAMINATION BY MR GREGGERY
MR GREGGERY: Ms Campbell, you were served with a Notice to give a Statement and
Produce Documents NTG-0057 dated 24 October 2022?
MS CAMPBELL: Yes, Counsel.
MR GREGGERY: And you provided a Statement in Response dated 25 October 2022?
MS CAMPBELL: That's my understanding. I'm just trying to -
MR GREGGERY: That's your recollection, yes. And you were also provided with a Notice to
give a Statement and Produce Documents NTG-0043 dated 26 October 2022, and you

MS CAMPBELL: Yes.
MR GREGGERY: Thank you. Commissioner, I tender both Notices and Statements, which
appear on the draft list as Exhibits 1744 through to 1747. There are additional documents
which will be tendered also, which appear on the draft list from 1748 through to 2029.
COMMISSIONER: All right. Those documents will be admitted as Exhibits with the numbers
they bear in the schedule. Thank you.
<EXHIBITS 1748 THROUGH TO 2029 TENDERED AS PER THE DRAFT LIST
MR GREGGERY: Thank you, Commissioner. Ms Campbell, the Commission heard some
evidence on Monday from Mr McNamara who came to work in the Department in respect of
the Ombudsman's inquiry in January 2017?
MS CAMPBELL: I think Mr McNamara came to work in a broader range in the compliance
area. I don't think it was just for the Ombudsman's report.
MR GREGGERY: Certainly.
MS CAMPBELL: Yes.
MR GREGGERY: He gave some evidence about your personal characteristics as a Secretary
and some observations he made of you from that point forward. He described you as a
detailed person, someone who focused on the detail. Would that be a fair observation?
MS CAMPBELL: I think during that period, I was very focused on the detail with respect to the
Scheme, yes.
MR GREGGERY: And that involved both media issues and compliance issues generally?
MS CAMPBELL: So I think it was - at that point in time, I was very focused on the Online
Compliance Initiative and the media attention that was being received from it, as well as the
broad range of the recipient experience and the entire program.
MR GREGGERY: Yes. He described that in respect of statements that went to the media or
the Minister, I think, that you were prepared to involve yourself in working over the language
and drafting various documents?
MS CAMPBELL: I think on some occasions, yes.
MR GREGGERY: Yes. All right. He used the phrase "hyper care" in terms of the sensitivity of
the OCI program in January 2017. Is that a phrase you're familiar with?
MS CAMPBELL: No.

MR GREGGERY: Right. And he also described the Department as “hierarchical”. Would you
agree that by virtue of the structure of it, it is necessarily hierarchical to some extent?
MS CAMPBELL: I think it is, particularly when there are about 35,000 people in the
Department, yes.
MR GREGGERY: And in respect of the OCI program particularly, there was - because of the
sensitivity of it in January 2017, and your involvement at the top of the hierarchy, the need
for a lot of information to be conveyed to you through that structure?
MS CAMPBELL: I think during that time, both myself and the then Minister were involved
with it, yes.
MR GREGGERY: Yes. And the then Minister, as I recall, was Minister Tudge?
MS CAMPBELL: That's correct.
MR GREGGERY: He returned from holidays on about 8 or 10 January 2017?
MS CAMPBELL: He did.
MR GREGGERY: And I think you returned from holidays at about that time as well?
MS CAMPBELL: I did.
MR GREGGERY: You may have come back early?
MS CAMPBELL: I did.
MR GREGGERY: From that point in time, whatever day it was, do you recall that you spent a
good deal of time with the Minister in his office reviewing aspects of the program with him,
including the media issues?
MS CAMPBELL: I think I spent significant amounts of time - often the Minister was down in
the Department as well.
MR GREGGERY: Right. Okay.
MS CAMPBELL: So, it wasn't just in his office. He - he was in the Department as well as we
worked through the issues and sought to rectify them.
MR GREGGERY: And in terms of your observation of the level of Minister Tudge's attention to
the matter, would you say that he was focused on the detail of the media as well as that
time?
MS CAMPBELL: He was focused on the detail of the program, which included the media.

MR GREGGERY: Yes. Right.
MS CAMPBELL: But he was also focused on the process, including from the recipient
experience.
MR GREGGERY: I'm aware of a speech you gave to an AAPA conference, or APAA conference,
where you described working on letters with Minister Tudge which went through a user
experience?
MS CAMPBELL: Yes. The IP - IPAA.
MR GREGGERY: IPAA.
MS CAMPBELL: I can't remember what that stands for, I'm sorry.
MR GREGGERY: That's all right.
MS CAMPBELL: Yes. We worked on some letters, yes.
MR GREGGERY: And where did that happen, in the DHS office or his office?
MS CAMPBELL: I think it was the DHS office.
MR GREGGERY: And these letters were letters that were being sent under the Scheme to
recipients?
MS CAMPBELL: These were letters that we were working on to improve the letters that were
being sent to the recipients, yes.
MR GREGGERY: And in that process, did you and he work out or revise the phrasing in the
letters, that sort of thing?
MS CAMPBELL: I think on one occasion we did, and then that letter was tested with
recipients. And -
MR GREGGERY: And it ended up not making its way into the final version, I -
MS CAMPBELL: No, it didn't.
MR GREGGERY: But it reflected the level of detail that Minister Tudge had in respect of the
program generally?
MS CAMPBELL: I think it reflected at that point in time, in the first weeks of January, the
need to improve the process and that both the Minister and I had engaged with that process.
I think that example I gave during the IPAA speech was one that sometimes the intent was
that - of that comment - was that sometimes it's best left to others to do that type of work

and - and to also understand that citizens sometimes come at things from a different way,
and using the co-design and testing of such letters was a beneficial process.
MR GREGGERY: Because, ordinarily, it wouldn't be the case that the Minister would settle
letters together with the Secretary which is sent out to recipients?
MS CAMPBELL: No. But - but letters are a very contentious issue in the then Department of
Human Services. And even now, in Services Australia, letters are something that there is
significant debate about.
MR GREGGERY: Yes. You made reference on the previous occasion when you gave evidence
to the Administrative Arrangements Orders and the areas of responsibility for the
Department of Human Services?
MS CAMPBELL: Yes.
MR GREGGERY: If Exhibit 1985, RBD.9999.0001.0045, would be produced. I'm just having the
page number turned up. But, Ms Campbell, you will recognise, I think, the front page of the
Administrative Arrangements Order dated 23 December 2014?
MS CAMPBELL: Yes, Counsel.
MR GREGGERY: And as the Commission has seen through other witnesses, including
Mr Pratt, this is a comprehensive document which is issued almost always in respect of all
government Departments and all administration administered by those Departments?
MS CAMPBELL: That's correct.
MS HOGAN-DORAN: If it's convenient, Exhibits 1985 through to 1990 could be tendered.
COMMISSIONER: Do you want to do that?
MR GREGGERY: Yes.
COMMISSIONER: And, look, just while we are on the subject of exhibits, 1744 actually was an
exhibit yesterday already. So the Notice to Give a Statement which I had earlier said could
have that number will now be 1744A.
MR GREGGERY: If we could just skip through the pages until we reach the Department of
Human Services. At page 26 appears the orders relevant to the Department of which you
were the Secretary, Ms Campbell?
MS CAMPBELL: Yes.
MR GREGGERY: It identifies there that the matters dealt with by the Department are the
development, delivery and coordination of government services and development of policy

MS CAMPBELL: In that version, yes, that was the case. Yes.
MR GREGGERY: That's right. There were changes to the terms of the Administrative
Arrangements Orders over successive orders?
MS CAMPBELL: There was.
MR GREGGERY: But I think this was the version as it was - which was current at the time OCI
was introduced?
MS CAMPBELL: Yes.
MR GREGGERY: It also refers to monitoring and management of service delivery
arrangements involving social security. You gave evidence at the last occasion that the
Department, that is, DHS, had responsibility for ensuring the legality of service delivery?
MS CAMPBELL: Yes.
MR GREGGERY: Or lawfulness of service delivery?
MS CAMPBELL: I - I can go to the transcript to just see exactly what I said there.
MR GREGGERY: It might be at page 961.
MS CAMPBELL: 961?
MR GREGGERY: Yes. About lines 30, I think.
MS CAMPBELL: And your question to me was:
Including the lawfulness of the method of implementation?
And I answered:
Yes.
MR GREGGERY: Yes.
MS CAMPBELL: Yes.
MR GREGGERY: And that is a reflection of the Administrative Arrangements Orders which
designate responsibility for social service delivery to DHS?
MS CAMPBELL: Yes. And - yes.

MR GREGGERY: There may be some other statutory requirements under the Public Service
Act or the Public Governance, Performance and Accountability Act. But in any event, your
answer derives from the terms of the Administrative Arrangements Orders?
MS CAMPBELL: Yes. And - and I read that with the - when looking at lawfulness, the - how we
implemented the program.
MR GREGGERY: Yes. The reference there to the development of policy on service delivery
includes, in this case, the policy which surrounds the delivery of the OCI program?
MS CAMPBELL: The delivery.
MR GREGGERY: Yes. And included in the delivery of the OCI program was the basis on which
debts were calculated and money was recovered?
MS CAMPBELL: Yes. How - how it was implemented, yes.
MR GREGGERY: That's right, yes.
MS CAMPBELL: Yes.
MR GREGGERY: The information that you obtained through Ms Golightly in the development
of the 12 February 2015 Executive Minute to Minister Morrison, did you understand from
that information that there were policy concerns from DSS about the implementation of the
proposal as it was then understood?
MS CAMPBELL: I understood that DSS had wanted to continue to work in that proposal -
MR GREGGERY: Yes.
MS CAMPBELL: - and that the advice we were giving to the Minister for Social Services was
that we would continue to pursue those issues with Social Services.
MR GREGGERY: And those issues were the question of legislative change and/or policy
change?
MS CAMPBELL: That's right.
MR GREGGERY: Thank you. If -
MS CAMPBELL: I just ask whether we could turn that light down as well. I just realised there's
another light.
MR GREGGERY: If Exhibit 2028 could be placed on the screen. I'm going to take you to the
Executive Minute itself in full form, Ms Campbell. CTH.2004.0002.2505. Commissioner, I
understand there was late agreement on the inclusion of the document -

COMMISSIONER: I think that it will -
MR GREGGERY: - which might explain why the document manager is loading the document.
COMMISSIONER: But it is coming?
MR GREGGERY: It is coming. Thank you. Ms Campbell, on the screen is Exhibit 2028, which is
the cover email for attachment B15125, Deputy Secretary Signed Brief. That was the 12
February 2015 Executive Minute from DHS to Minister Morrison for action?
MS CAMPBELL: I don't know whether that's the case or not.
MR GREGGERY: Okay.
MS CAMPBELL: I don't think I'm copied in on that Brief.
MR GREGGERY: You're not copied in, no.
MS CAMPBELL: So I have no way of knowing, I'm sorry, and I haven't been able to see that
document in the lead-up to today.
MR GREGGERY: Okay. Perhaps if we go, then, to Exhibit 2029, CTH.2004.0002.2506, the
attachment. While that's coming up, Ms Campbell, in terms of your involvement in the
preparation of the Executive Minute, I recall you gave evidence that you were involved in the
various drafts of the Executive Minute to Minister Morrison, together with Ms Golightly?
MS CAMPBELL: I was involved in a number of drafts. I can't say whether that was every draft.
Because I would have to have a look at each and every one to make sure that they were the
case. So the ones from my review of my emails I have discovered and the documents that I
was involved with some of the drafts, yes. And then I would have been copied in on the
distribution list at the top of the final one.
MR GREGGERY: That's right. So we can see the reference there in the top right-hand corner
to your position. If we can scroll down to page 4. Ms Campbell, you can see there, following
paragraph 23, the signature of Ms Golightly, although it's been blacked out, and the date, 12
February 2015?
MS CAMPBELL: Yes.
MR GREGGERY: Now, the final version, then, of the minute was something, as you say, that
was copied to you?
MS CAMPBELL: Yes.
MR GREGGERY: And do you recall asking - answering questions that I asked about this
Executive Minute on the previous occasion?

MS CAMPBELL: I remember answering questions, yes, Counsel.
MR GREGGERY: And you might recall that the document about which I questioned you
contained Mr Morrison's signature of various highlighting and circling in respect of options to
progress matters or discuss matters or not to proceed with matters?
MS CAMPBELL: I do recall that, yes.
MR GREGGERY: Yes. Do you recall also that there were 11 pages of the document that I
showed you last time with Minister Morrison's signature on it?
MS CAMPBELL: I don't recall that.
MR GREGGERY: All right. You may take it from me that there was only 11 pages. This copy
contains all 17 pages. And if we go back to page 1, ending 2506. Thank you. Ms Campbell,
you can see in the box of recommendations, item 3 is a request to:
Note the current arrangements to maintain the integrity of welfare payment outlays
(Attachment B).
And then go to page 12 of 17. You can see in the top right corner, Attachment B. And it is a
total of six pages through to page 17 of 17. I will take you to some specific portions of it
firstly, but - and you may recall them from previous drafts in any event that were exchanged
with Minister Payne. But, Commissioner, I can explain that the missing pages in the previous
Hearing Block have been explained now by correspondence which indicates that the
Minister's Office, that's Minister Morrison's Office or Minister Morrison, retained
Attachment B and it wasn't returned to the Department.
COMMISSIONER: Oh, I see. All right.
MR GREGGERY: And the emails which reflect that position at the time the attachment in part
was returned or the Minute in part was returned will be tendered.
COMMISSIONER: Thank you.
MR GREGGERY: The passages to which I want you - I want to have your attention drawn, Ms
Campbell, commence at page 13 of 17, ending 2518, at paragraph 12. And if paragraph 12
could firstly be called out. I'm going to ask you to read just to yourself through to paragraph
23, and we will just deal with the paragraphs sequentially.
MS CAMPBELL: I'm ready to move to the next page. Thank you.
MR GREGGERY: Thank you, Ms Campbell.
MS CAMPBELL: I'm ready to move to the next part. Thank you.

MS CAMPBELL: I've finished reading up to paragraph 20.
MR GREGGERY: Thank you.
MS CAMPBELL: I'm ready to move on. Thank you.
MR GREGGERY: Just through to the end of paragraph 23. Thank you, Ms Campbell.
MS CAMPBELL: Thank you.
MR GREGGERY: Thank you. Ms Campbell, do you recall working on a draft with Ms Golightly
which contained effectively the same information?
MS CAMPBELL: I recall - now that I've been able to look at the data and look at the
information, I recall working on this. But - I recall it at that point in time, yes. But it's not
something - the detail of every brief, unfortunately, don't remain with me until I have my
memory refreshed.
MR GREGGERY: Certainly. If we could go back to paragraph 14. It identifies a response to a
problem which is set out earlier, but it identifies inconsistencies between information
customers had given to different areas of government, and paragraph 15 refers to PAYG
information. The two letters which recipients received under the OCI program, the first of
which has been described on a number of occasions as the identification of a discrepancy, is
that language familiar to you?
MS CAMPBELL: Yes.
MR GREGGERY: And here in paragraph 14, the word "inconsistency" is used, but I gather it's
the same concept?
MS CAMPBELL: Yes.
MR GREGGERY: The concept of a discrepancy, as it was identified in the original letters, that
is, the initial letter sent to customers under the OCI program, must have resulted from some
comparison of information held by DHS and information from the ATO?
MS CAMPBELL: Yes.
MR GREGGERY: And the information held by DHS, I take it, would have been reporting during
fortnightly periods when persons received an income support supplement?
MS CAMPBELL: Yes.
MR GREGGERY: And the information from the ATO, I understand, is the PAYG summaries
which are provided by the ATO to DHS?

MS CAMPBELL: Yes.
MR GREGGERY: And in order for an inconsistency or a discrepancy to be identified, as you've
indicated, there was a comparison between those two data sources. Did it involve the
application of an initial concept of averaging in respect of the PAYG summary to the
information reported by the recipient to Centrelink?
MS CAMPBELL: My understanding, it was over the period that the ATO had reported that
those earnings had been achieved. So if it was over a three-month period, there was an
averaging over the three-month period. If it was a 12-month period, it was an averaging over
a 12-month period.
MR GREGGERY: All right. And what is reflected, I think, in Attachment A, which I took you to
last time, is that the application of that concept of inconsistency was not a new feature of
the program, but the concept of the PAYG data being the primary source of information to
establish a discrepancy was a new step in the OCI program?
MS CAMPBELL: I think I answered last time that it - in the manual system, it had been one
element.
MR GREGGERY: Yes.
MS CAMPBELL: It had often been in the manual system. The reason why a manual
compliance had been undertaken was that -
MR GREGGERY: A trigger point.
MS CAMPBELL: It was a trigger point, yes.
MR GREGGERY: But here, that is, under this proposal - and I appreciate it's a proposal at this
point, the Scheme is not implemented - the proposal was that the trigger point would not be
a trigger point for a manual investigation within Centrelink but a trigger point for the initial
letter?
MS CAMPBELL: Yes.
MR GREGGERY: And that, in the event that the customer responded to the initial letter, their
information would be taken into account, in part manually, on a review process?
MS CAMPBELL: Yes. And I think the intent was that we were encouraging as many people as
possible to respond to us.
MR GREGGERY: And in the event that a customer didn't respond, that initial averaging, which
triggered the initial letter, was applied to arrive at a debt or not?
MS CAMPBELL: After a reminder letter. And I think my Statement indicated that I was

MR GREGGERY: Yes. But ultimately, in terms of what information was provided or not, where
information was not provided, for whatever reason, by a recipient or intended recipient of
the letters, the initial data match was effectively crystallised into the final position and
reflected?
MS CAMPBELL: And that was the initial rollout, and that's why sought to change that after
we were aware of the shortfalls in the initial rollout.
MR GREGGERY: Yes. All right. And so would you agree with me, then, that one change in the
proposal - just dealing with it at this stage - was the change from the trigger for an internal
review versus the trigger for the initial letter?
MS CAMPBELL: Yes.
MR GREGGERY: The problem which was identified in paragraph 14 was set out in more detail
in paragraph 12 and paragraph 13, and it identifies there - or it is identified there that
welfare claimants have variable circumstances, essentially, and there are complexities to the
reporting arrangements and the receipt of benefits?
MS CAMPBELL: It is a very complex system, and that was identified here.
MR GREGGERY: Yes. And the reporting of changes in circumstances to real-life situations can
make it difficult to comply with the rules, even where there is a desire to do so. That's a
reflection of the complex system?
MS CAMPBELL: That's right.
MR GREGGERY: And it's a key driving factor according to the proposal of levels of customer
error?
MS CAMPBELL: That's - as per that paragraph. That's what that paragraph says.
MR GREGGERY: Yes. Now, returning then to paragraph 14, the shortcomings in the PAYG
data were identified in the second paragraph, commencing with the sentence:
However, the range of data –
If that could be called out. Or if not, perhaps expanded a little. Thank you.
The range of data currently matched against –
That's a reference to what you just described as the information reported to Centrelink by
the recipient and the PAYG data?
MS CAMPBELL: Yes.

MR GREGGERY: And the variability and timeliness and quality, firstly in respect of timeliness,
is a reflection of the periods which PAYG data can be reported by employers to the ATO?
MS CAMPBELL: That's my understanding of that, yes.
MR GREGGERY: And it can have, then, an effect on the quality or the ability to use the PAYG
data in a more timely and efficient manner?
MS CAMPBELL: That's what the paragraph indicates.
MR GREGGERY: That's what the paragraph says. And one of those features is because it is, to
your understanding, I suggest, only a requirement on employers to report the PAYG data
close to the end of the financial year?
MS CAMPBELL: I don't - I'm not aware of that.
MR GREGGERY: You're not aware of that. The reference to the limits in respect of legislation
and policy - at least legislation we have addressed before - that related to the ability to use
PAYG data on an average basis as evidence of actual income during a fortnightly period?
MS CAMPBELL: Yes, we discussed that last time.
MR GREGGERY: And the policy questions - if I can address those with you now. Would you
agree that in respect of the concept of averaging PAYG data and using it as actual evidence of
fortnightly income that there is likely to be a variation between the averaged figure and the
actual income figure for any particular fortnight?
MS CAMPBELL: There could be, depending on the circumstances of the employment. If the
recipient who is reporting was working the same pattern, it's possible that the amounts
could have been equal. If they were working irregular hours, it is possible that it wouldn't.
MR GREGGERY: And so in respect of casual workers, there was a risk that the averaged
income would not reflect actual income?
MS CAMPBELL: That was the case, yes.
MR GREGGERY: And with seasonal workers?
MS CAMPBELL: Seasonal workers had a different - there were different rules around seasonal
workers. I can't recall what they are now, but there are different rules in the Social Security
Act about seasonal work.
MR GREGGERY: But for example, if someone worked six months of the year in a fruit-picking
season and then didn't have employment for the following six months of the financial year
but an employer reported their PAYG summary for the whole of the financial year, the
average would be inconsistent with actual earnings?

MS CAMPBELL: Not wanting to be pedantic, but there is a clause in the Social Security Act
about seasonal workers. And I cannot recall what it is, but I know that seasonal work - my
recollection is that seasonal work is treated differently.
MR GREGGERY: All right.
MS CAMPBELL: So if we could use a different example.
MR GREGGERY: What about a university student who works on holidays and weekends and
their work fluctuates around their studies and exams?
MS CAMPBELL: Yes, it - it may not reflect accurately what the weekly -
MR GREGGERY: Yes.
COMMISSIONER: If it helps, Ms Campbell, I can tell you that on 9 March 2017, there was a
first tier AAT case of Jones decided which involved a shearer, whose work was effectively
seasonal, and his debt was set aside on the basis that averaging of income from nine
different employers for him had made no sense at all. So it does seem that whatever the
clause in the Social Security Act, people like that were caught by this Scheme.
MS CAMPBELL: I'm not denying that, Commissioner. It's just that I don't have the Social
Security Act here, and I just remembered there was something about the term "seasonal".
COMMISSIONER: Thank you.
MR GREGGERY: So, many of the persons who received Centrelink income support payments
would have variable work hours and variable incomes as a general proposition. Would you
accept that?
MS CAMPBELL: I do accept that there were - there was a significant cohort that would have
had variable.
MR GREGGERY: And they would be - that significant cohort would be captured by the risk of
the inaccurate calculation of actual fortnightly income by the averaging concept?
MS CAMPBELL: If they didn't have - if they weren't able to provide that alternate
information.
MR GREGGERY: But they would be caught by the initial averaging, which was what created
the discrepancy and led to the initial letter?
MS CAMPBELL: The trigger - the initial letter. And so, yes, they would have been sent an
initial letter.

MR GREGGERY: That's right. So they're caught initially by an averaging process. And then if
they don't respond, for whatever reason, that averaging process crystallises in respect of
that significant cohort and the risk is realised?
MS CAMPBELL: And so that was - we were - I was particularly worried in those first days
when it was rolled out that there hadn't been the opportunity for people to respond, that we
hadn't ensured that people received the letter, which is why there were changes, and that
the material wasn't clear enough on what was happening.
MR GREGGERY: I think you're agreeing with the proposition that where people didn't
respond, the risk of inaccurate calculations of fortnightly income would crystallise?
MS CAMPBELL: When people didn't respond, that's correct.
MR GREGGERY: Yes. And that in those circumstances, it would be obvious, I suggest, that the
allegation of a debt in a particular amount may well be unsustainable in fact.
MS CAMPBELL: Yes.
MR GREGGERY: And that would have been obvious at the time of this proposal because of
the recognised need for legislative and policy change?
MS CAMPBELL: This - so this document, which was the initial proposal -
MR GREGGERY: Yes.
MS CAMPBELL: - and then there would have been a final - new policy proposal that was
agreed. Yes.
MR GREGGERY: Yes. But the - what I have just identified with you as crystallisation of a debt
based on averaging not being supported in fact was an obvious feature of this proposal,
which is reflected in the alert to the Minister for the need for legislative and policy change?
MS CAMPBELL: That was an alert, yes.
MR GREGGERY: Yes. And the alert recognised the fact that averaging might not create, for a
significant cohort, an accurate fortnightly income?
MS CAMPBELL: Yes.
MR GREGGERY: And in some cases, that inaccuracy would be too high, that is, the averaging
process would lead to the allegation of a debt which was much higher than it had to be or
didn't exist at all?
MS CAMPBELL: Yes. And in some cases, debts that were lower if there hadn't been - if there
had been a manual process.

MR GREGGERY: Yes. And the concept of averaging PAYG data didn't take into account other
income which is non-reportable, as it were?
MS CAMPBELL: I'm sorry - such as?
MR GREGGERY: Well, there will be some case, would you agree, where the debt value
identified under a smoothed approach would be too high because excess income over the
fortnight disqualifying income level is currently ignored for single allowees, single
pensioners, partnered pension couples, whereas it would be included in the smoothed
approach? Would you agree with that?
MS CAMPBELL: I don't understand that, I'm sorry. If there is something that I could look at - I
don't understand what's being asked.
MR GREGGERY: Were you aware that in early 2015, a disqualifying amount for a single adult
Newstart recipient was $999 a fortnight, and for a single person on Youth Allowance under
18 years of age it was $545 a fortnight?
MS CAMPBELL: I don't know whether it was those exact amounts. I knew that there was an
